a: The time when DPR members don't hold meetings in Jakarta and instead go back to their home districts to meet residents.
The time when DPR members work in Jakarta: holding meetings, debating laws, and discussing the budget.
The area a DPR member represents, where they were elected in the general election.
The big meeting of all DPR members. The DPR's official decisions are made here, sealed with a gavel.
A meeting to hear input from outside the government: experts, organizations, ordinary citizens.
A DPR commission meeting with officials below minister level, such as the head of an agency or a director general.
A DPR commission meeting directly with a minister or the head of a minister-level agency.
A small team in the DPR that looks at one issue in more detail.
A special committee (panitia khusus): a temporary DPR team set up for one specific matter, for example a single bill.
A group of DPR members from the same party.
A DPR working group that handles a particular area. For example, Commission III handles legal affairs.
The part of the DPR that organizes and checks the drafting of laws.
The part of the DPR that discusses the state budget (APBN) together with the government.
The part of the DPR that receives complaints and aspirations directly from citizens.
A draft law (rancangan undang-undang): a future law that is still being discussed and is not yet in force.
A bill proposed by the DPR itself, not by the government.
The first round of deliberating a bill: it is discussed in detail in a commission or body together with the government.
The final round for a bill, held in the plenary meeting: it is either passed or not.
A list of responses to a draft bill, article by article.
A study document explaining why a bill is needed and what it contains.
The minimum number of people who must be present for a meeting to be valid.
Everyone agrees, with no vote.
A meeting is paused for a short while and will resume later.
A DPR test for candidates for official posts before they are approved.
The ministries or agencies that a DPR commission oversees.
The state budget for one year: how much money comes in and what it is spent on.
The regional government budget for one year.
The draft state budget (APBN) proposed by the government, before the DPR approves it.
Spending is bigger than income. The shortfall is covered by borrowing.
State income other than taxes, for example from mining, services, and fines.
Money from the state budget (APBN) that is sent to regional governments and villages.
Money from the central government to the regions that they can spend freely on basic needs, like staff salaries.
Money from the central government to the regions that can only be spent on specific activities.
The regions' share of taxes and mining revenue collected by the central government.
Leftover state money from previous years.
Spending required by law, for example at least 20 percent of the state budget (APBN) for education.
The Audit Board (Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan): the institution that audits how the state uses its money.
The government's own internal financial supervisor.
The BPK's six-monthly report card on its findings about how state money is used.
The best grade the BPK gives for a financial report (an unqualified opinion). It is not a guarantee of no corruption.
Public service that isn't done properly: slow, asking for money, playing favorites, or breaking procedure.
The official term for people serving a sentence in prison.
A correctional facility (lembaga pemasyarakatan), in other words, a prison.
A detention center (rumah tahanan): where people are held while their case is still being processed.
A surprise inspection: showing up to check without warning first.
Illegal levies (pungutan liar): asking for money outside the rules.
Part-time government contract workers, who don't work full hours and are paid less.
Government employees on work contracts, not civil servants (PNS).
The state civil apparatus (aparatur sipil negara): civil servants (PNS) and P3K contract employees.
Workers in government offices who don't yet have ASN status, usually with low pay.
An allowance for teachers who already hold an educator certificate.
Teacher professional education (pendidikan profesi guru), the path to getting an educator certificate.
The official database of schools, teachers, and students.
The National Education System, the name of the main law on education.
Combining several laws into one.
Seizing assets without waiting for the offender to be found guilty.
An official's wealth that rises unreasonably and whose origin can't be explained.
A legal action against the thing itself (the asset), not the person.
Acting honestly and not knowing there is a problem, for example buying something without knowing it came from a crime.
A fair legal process: there is evidence, there is a judge, and there is a chance to defend yourself.
A wanted persons list (daftar pencarian orang), in other words, fugitives.
An international request through Interpol to find a fugitive.
Money laundering (tindak pidana pencucian uang): disguising the origin of money gained from crime.
The Criminal Code: the list of prohibited acts and their punishments.
The Criminal Procedure Code: the rules for how a criminal case proceeds, from investigation to trial.
The Constitutional Court, which checks whether a law complies with the 1945 Constitution. Its rulings must be followed.
A court ruling that is already final and can no longer be appealed.
Makan Bergizi Gratis, the government's free meals program.
The total Hajj pilgrimage cost per pilgrim, partly paid by the pilgrim and partly from the Hajj managed funds.
The supervisory board (dewan pengawas) of an institution.
The Chief of the Indonesian National Police, the top commander of the police.
A state institution that oversees public services and receives complaints from citizens.
Safeguards or limits in a regulation (literally "five fences"), meant to stop officials from abusing it.
